cur:manuscripts-egberti-peters-mother-in.summary: Christ, labelled IHS XPS and followed by his apostles, reaches toward a woman lying sick on a green couch before a house, while a man behind her raises his hands. The story of the healing in Peter's house is told with a few large, expressive figures.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.

Egbert gave the book to the church of St Paulin in Trier, where it was used in services until the 18th century; it has been in the Trier city library since 1810 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2004 with other Reichenau manuscripts.

cur:monumental-john-vii-oratory-magi.summary: The Virgin, robed in deep blue, sits on a cushioned throne holding the Christ Child, who leans forward to receive a gift from a kneeling magus in a red cloak; Joseph and an angel stand behind. This fragment is one of the few survivors of the mosaics of the oratory built by Pope John VII in Old St Peter's, demolished during the rebuilding of the basilica in the early 17th century.
facts: Pope John VII (705–707) built an oratory dedicated to the Virgin inside Old St Peter's; its mosaics were removed when the old basilica was demolished, and fragments are now scattered among several churches and the Vatican Grottoes.
Another fragment from the same oratory, showing the bathing of the Christ Child, is also in the collection.

cur:monumental-sma-christ-among-seraphim.summary: In the semi-dome of the apse, the faded figure of Christ stands frontally, his right hand raised in blessing, surrounded by seraphim, with saints and the figure of Pope Paul I below. Painted over earlier decoration, the apse shows how successive popes renewed the church's sanctuary.
facts: Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum preserves wall paintings from the 6th to the late 8th century; buried after an earthquake in 847, it was rediscovered only in 1900.
The apse was repainted under Pope Paul I (757–767), whose decorations at Santa Maria Antiqua use Latin inscriptions only.

cur:monumental-cavusin-adoration-of-magi.summary: The Virgin, robed in deep red and seated on a tall jewelled throne, holds the Christ Child on her lap as the Magi in rich red mantles approach with their gifts from the right; an angel above guides them. Painted in strong reds, greens and whites, the scene belongs to the continuous Gospel cycle that covers the walls of this imperially connected church.
facts: The church at Çavuşin, the 'Pigeon House' church, includes portraits of Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas and his wife Theophano, which allow it to be dated unusually precisely to 963–969.
An on-site plan (photographed on Commons) lists thirty scenes in the church, running from the prophetic vision and the Annunciation through the Passion to the Ascension.

cur:objects-berlin-pyxis-christ-among-di.summary: Around this ivory box a youthful, beardless Christ sits on a high-backed throne, teaching from an open scroll, while the apostles stand or sit around him in animated discussion, like philosophers around a master. The other side of the pyxis shows Abraham about to sacrifice Isaac, the Old Testament prefiguration of Christ's sacrifice. The classical poise of the figures makes this one of the most beautiful of all Early Christian ivories.
facts: Christ enthroned as teacher among the apostles was one of the favourite images of Christ in the late 4th and early 5th centuries, borrowed from the iconography of philosophers and their pupils (type).
The museum label describes its origin as unknown and dates it to about 400.

vam:O116028.summary: Printed in indigo on linen, this fragmentary panel shows the Virgin Mary reclining on a couch at the centre, with a winged angel standing at the left and, at the right, the remains of the raised manger with traces of the ox and the ass above it. Beside the Virgin's head a damaged Greek inscription names her MAPIA (Maria), and a small star shines near by. The Christ Child, who presumably lay in the manger, is now lost in the damaged area, but the panel remains a precious survival of Nativity imagery on an everyday textile from late Roman Egypt.
facts: The V&A places the panel in a group of resist-dyed textiles found at Akhmîm and Antinoë in Egypt and now scattered among many museums; some were already old when they were reused to pad out mummy wrappings.
According to the museum, the Virgin's relaxed pose on her couch is that of a Roman matron, and the rectangular scene framed by columns recalls the side of a Roman sarcophagus.

The resist (possibly wax) was block-printed onto the linen before it was dipped in indigo; the presence of the angel at the birth follows the eastern tradition of texts such as the Protevangelium of James.
vam:O116028.notes: The figure of the Christ Child is not visible: the V&A states that the manger 'presumably contained the Christ Child'. The identification of the scene as the Nativity is secure (inscription MAPIA, angel, ox and ass, manger). Dated 4th century by the V&A. From the Major Myers collection, given by Dudley B. Myers.
